title: Multimodal Models & Evaluation
blurb: Tests CLIP's symmetric contrastive loss and why both directions matter, zero-shot classification by text prompts, CLIPScore, FID and Inception Score, sanity-checking a new metric, and the limits of metrics built on a feature extractor.

refLinks.label: §74.2.1 Contrastive Alignment Forces Genuine Correspondence, Not Memorization
§74.2.2 Zero-Shot Classification Is the Direct Payoff of a Shared Space
§74.2.3 CLIPScore Is the Training Objective, Reused as a Metric
§74.2.4 FID and Inception Score Use a Feature Extractor as a Stand-In for “Looks Real”

questions.prompt: What does CLIP train its two encoders to do?
options: Pull matched pairs together, push mismatches apart
Translate captions into a second language
Reconstruct each image from its caption, pixel by pixel
Predict a fixed class label for each image and caption
questions.explanation: No class labels are involved, only which pairs belong together. That's why any prompt can be compared with any image afterwards.

questions.prompt: With a batch of 128 pairs, what loss does an untrained, random-similarity CLIP model start at? Give four decimal places.
questions.explanation: Each row is a 128-way classification with a uniform guess, so the loss is ln 128 = 4.8520. Procedure 74.1 uses this as a check on the loss code.

questions.prompt: Why does clip_loss normalise embeddings before the dot product?
options: Normalising makes the batch size irrelevant to the loss.
Otherwise it can cheat by inflating vector magnitudes.
It halves the memory the similarity matrix needs.
The cross-entropy function only accepts unit vectors.
questions.explanation: Unit vectors turn the dot product into cosine similarity, so only direction counts. That's the procedure's common mistake.

questions.prompt: Why is the CLIP loss applied in both directions, image-to-text and text-to-image?
options: The text encoder can't receive gradients otherwise.
One direction alone lets the text side drift.
Two directions double the batch size for free.
It makes the temperature parameter unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The symmetric loss forces a shared, mutually consistent space for both encoders.

refLinks.label: §74.2.1 Contrastive Alignment Forces Genuine Correspondence, Not Memorization

questions.prompt: How does CLIP classify an image zero-shot?
options: Generate a caption, then match it to a label list.
Embed a prompt per class and pick the closest.
Add a new classifier head and fine-tune it briefly.
Retrain the image encoder on the new classes.
questions.explanation: No head and no fine-tuning. Class prompts are embedded once and compared with each image.

refLinks.label: §74.2.2 Zero-Shot Classification Is the Direct Payoff of a Shared Space

questions.prompt: Why do real deployments average several prompt templates per class?
options: CLIP can't read prompts shorter than five words.
Each template trains the model further.
Prompt wording changes zero-shot accuracy.
Averaging removes the need for normalisation.
questions.explanation: Prompt ensembling smooths over wording effects. Inconsistent templates across classes is the procedure's common mistake.

questions.prompt: What does the 96.9% zero-shot accuracy on held-out digits show?
options: The model memorised each canonical prompt during training.
The task was too easy to measure anything.
Its alignment generalises to unseen prompts.
CLIP-style models always beat task-specific classifiers.
questions.explanation: Training used three varied templates, never the canonical prompts as fixed targets. The trade-offs section notes a task-specific model usually wins on its own task.

options: The fraction of captions CLIP generates correctly
Cosine similarity of image and caption embeddings
The accuracy of a classifier trained on CLIP features
The Fréchet distance between image and text features
questions.explanation: It reuses the training signal as a metric, and needs no reference image, only the pair being judged.

refLinks.label: §74.2.3 CLIPScore Is the Training Objective, Reused as a Metric

questions.prompt: Which direction is better for FID and for Inception Score?
options: Higher FID is better. Lower Inception Score is better.
Higher is better for both.
Lower is better for both.
Lower FID, higher IS
questions.explanation: FID is a distance from real data. IS rewards sharp per-image predictions and broad variety.

refLinks.label: §74.2.4 FID and Inception Score Use a Feature Extractor as a Stand-In for “Looks Real”

options: High similarity between each image and its caption
Sharp per-image predictions and broad variety
Images that look like the average of the training set
Low distance between generated and real feature means
questions.explanation: IS = exp(E[KL(p(y|x) ‖ p(y))]). Sharp p(y|x) and broad p(y) both raise it.

refLinks.label: §74.2.4 FID and Inception Score Use a Feature Extractor as a Stand-In for “Looks Real”

questions.prompt: Why isn't zero the practical floor for FID?
options: The trace term can never reach zero.
Zero needs infinite samples, so use real-vs-real.
FID is always at least 1 by construction.
Zero would mean the feature extractor failed.
questions.explanation: Two finite splits of the same data still differ. Their FID is the realistic best case to compare against.

refLinks.label: §74.2.4 FID and Inception Score Use a Feature Extractor as a Stand-In for “Looks Real”

questions.prompt: What does Procedure 74.6 check before a new metric is trusted?
options: It gives the same value on two different GPUs.
It runs in under a second per image.
It worsens steadily from real to noise.
It agrees with a human rating on ten images.
questions.explanation: fid_baseline < fid_degraded < fid_noise. If the order fails, debug the metric before using it.

questions.prompt: FID rose from 0.62 to 1.88 to 5.72 while Inception Score fell from 8.77 to 5.25 to 3.15 across the same three conditions. Why is that agreement meaningful?
options: Both metrics are computed from the same formula.
The numbers prove the generator is perfect.
Two unrelated formulas told the same story.
It shows FID and IS are interchangeable.
questions.explanation: Gaussian distribution distance and classifier-confidence entropy agreeing is a real cross-check, not a redundancy.

questions.prompt: Why are FID, Inception Score and CLIPScore proxies rather than ground truth?
options: They can only be computed during training.
Each inherits its feature extractor's blind spots.
They are computed on too few images to mean anything.
They ignore the images and use only captions.
questions.explanation: That's why computing two structurally different metrics and checking agreement is standard practice.

questions.prompt: A team plans to train a CLIP-scale model from scratch for a general text-to-image feature. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Use a managed or pretrained model, and fine-tune only for truly domain-specific data.
Skip evaluation metrics, since pretrained models are already validated.
Train from scratch, since it gives the most control.
Train a small toy model, since the mechanism carries over at any scale.
questions.explanation: Real CLIP trained on hundreds of millions of pairs. Bedrock or JumpStart are the practical entry points. Toy models validate the mechanism, not the scale.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain why CLIP's contrastive loss is trained in both directions (image-to-text and text-to-image) rather than image-to-text alone, using the collapse failure mode described in the Exposition.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If trained image-to-text only, the loss could be minimized by collapsing all text embeddings toward a single point near any plausible image embedding (satisfying "does this text match this image" without penalizing "does this image match other texts"). Training both directions symmetrically forces every image and every text to be individually well-separated in both directions simultaneously, preventing that collapse.

bookExercises.prompt: State, in one sentence, why zero-shot classification requires no classifier head, referencing Listing 74.2.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Zero-shot classification requires no classifier head because the class labels are themselves embedded as text through CLIP's existing text encoder, and classification becomes similarity comparison between the image embedding and each class's text embedding. No new weights need to be trained for a specific label set.

bookExercises.prompt: Using this chapter's measured first-epoch loss (4.2165) and the `ln(batch_size)` diagnostic from Procedure 74.1, compute what the expected first-epoch loss would be if the batch size were changed from 64 to 128, and state whether a first-epoch loss far from that new value should be blamed on the model or the loss implementation.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Chance-level loss is $\ln(N)$; for $N=128$, expected loss is $\ln(128) \approx 4.852$, compared to $\ln(64) \approx 4.159$ measured. A first-epoch loss far from this new expected chance level (either much higher or, oddly, much lower) should generally be blamed on the loss implementation (e.g. a bug in the similarity matrix construction or target indexing) rather than the model, since an untrained model at epoch 0 is expected to sit close to chance-level loss almost by construction.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 74.4 and this chapter's measured FID table, explain why the real-vs-real split (0.6201) is not exactly zero, and what would need to change about the dataset for it to approach zero.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The real-vs-real FID (0.6201) is not exactly zero because it compares two different random splits of a finite dataset. Even genuinely identical distributions produce nonzero FID when estimated from finite, different samples (sampling noise in the mean/covariance estimates). For it to approach zero, the dataset would need to grow much larger (reducing estimation variance) or the two splits would need to become the same images (which would defeat the sanity-check's purpose).

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 74.6, describe what conclusion should be drawn if Step 2 (real vs. degraded) produced a *lower* FID than Step 1 (real vs. real), and what the most likely cause would be.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If Step 2 (real vs. degraded) produced a lower FID than Step 1 (real vs. real), that would indicate a bug in the FID implementation itself, since degraded images should be *more* dissimilar to real images than real images are to a different random split of themselves. FID is expected to be monotonically ordered (real-vs-real lowest, degraded next, pure noise highest), and a violation of that ordering points to an error in the feature extraction, covariance computation, or `sqrtm` step, not a genuine finding about the images.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer wants to evaluate a newly fine-tuned text-to-image model and proposes reporting only Inception Score, since it needs no separate real reference set and is cheaper to compute. Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you would say to them about that proposal.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Inception Score doesn't require a real reference set, which is convenient, but per this chapter's Trade-offs, it can't detect whether the generated distribution actually resembles real data. It only checks whether individual predictions are confident and collectively diverse, both of which a model could satisfy while still looking nothing like real images. I'd recommend at minimum pairing it with FID, which directly compares to a real reference set, before trusting IS alone as ship/no-ship evidence."

bookExercises.prompt: A customer's product needs to classify images into a label set that changes weekly. Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, explain in two or three sentences why zero-shot CLIP-style classification is a better starting point than retraining a fixed classifier head each week, and what it would cost them in peak accuracy.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Zero-shot CLIP-style classification requires no retraining when the label set changes, just re-embed the new text prompts, which is a much faster and cheaper response to a weekly-changing label set than retraining a fixed classifier head from scratch each week. The cost is typically some peak accuracy versus a purpose-trained classifier on a fixed label set, since the zero-shot approach isn't specialized to your exact categories the way a dedicated trained head would be."

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Hessel et al. CLIPScore paper cited above. Identify one way real CLIPScore differs from this chapter's Procedure 74.3, and explain what problem that difference solves at real deployment scale.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Real CLIPScore (Hessel et al.) is typically computed with a much larger, pretrained CLIP model over open-vocabulary captions, and the paper also proposes a reference-augmented variant (RefCLIPScore) combining it with similarity to human reference captions when available. This chapter's Procedure 74.3 uses the toy CLIP trained on a small fixed vocabulary. The difference matters at production scale because a small, closed-vocabulary toy encoder cannot generalize its similarity judgments to captions or images outside its narrow training distribution the way a large pretrained model can.
